findings.title: Consent had eight implementations across six domains and no stated canonical owner
findings.description: Seven ORM classes map seven distinct *consent* tables (consents, niam_consents, niam_lifecycle_consents, trust_consent_records, dp_consent_directives, national_consents, rp_consent_records) and an eighth implementation, citizen_platform.privacy.ConsentEngine, is not an ORM model at all. findings.root_cause: Consent was modelled independently by each domain that needed it, with no constitution naming which store an authorization decision must consult.
findings.evidence: Cached 829-class ownership scan re-queried for 'consent': 7 ORM classes, 7 tables, 6 domains, zero duplicate table ownership. Migration search by table name: only 4 of 7 are built (consents 20260417_0001, niam_consents 20260814_0006, niam_lifecycle_consents 20260723_0002, trust_consent_records 20260716_0013); the other 3 are ORM-only and all three are already declared in test_schema_fidelity's unbuilt ledger. Decisive evidence for ownership: exactly one implementation is wired into an authorization decision -- security/consent_dep.py::require_consent is a route dependency guarding services/mpi/api.py:316, and it queries `consents` via services/consent_service.py. It is also the only one that audits: log_access_decision writes an AuditLog row on all five decision branches (owner bypass, emergency denied, emergency allowed, no-consent deny, allow). Subject/tenancy columns measured per table: consents keys on gpid (citizen ULID) + grantee_id with no tenant column; trust_consent_records is the only one carrying lab_id.

findings.title: CLAUDE.md requires every mutation to be audited; 328 mutating endpoints are in packages with no audit call at all, and 1065 are in modules with none
findings.description: The audit architecture itself is sound and needs no redesign: services/audit_service.py chains each entry as SHA-256(previous_chain_hash + record), anchors it off-database under an HMAC (AUDIT_ANCHOR_KEY) and can re-verify the chain (verify_audit_chain). That is tamper-evident. Coverage is the gap. Of 1222 mutating endpoints (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) across 42 packages, 271 (22%) are in 25 packages containing no audit call anywhere. Corrected in Unit 4: the original 271/25 figure was produced by a detector matching its tokens as plain substrings, which counted `query_audit_log(`, `access_audit_log(`, `get_audit_log(` (app/control_plane -- three read helpers) and `_write_audit` (app/governance) as canonical audit calls. Word-boundary matching restores both packages: 27 packages, 328 endpoints. Measured per module instead of per package, 130 of the 160 modules containing a mutating endpoint contain no audit call, covering 1065 of 1222 endpoints -- the upper bound, now ratcheted alongside the lower one.
findings.root_cause: The rule is stated in CLAUDE.md but enforced nowhere mechanically: auditing is a call each author must remember to make, at the layer furthest from the mutation.
findings.evidence: AST scan of app/ counting POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE route decorators per package, against a broad token search for audit participation. 271 unaudited mutating endpoints across 25 packages is the LOWER bound -- 'the package audits somewhere' does not prove a given endpoint audits. A module-level pass gives the upper bound: 435 of 527 route-module endpoints (83%) are in modules that never name an audit call. Both are proxies and are reported as such. Highest-count unaudited packages: payments 34, capabilities 29, document_intelligence 25, ai_fabric 23, blood_bank 21, research_platform 16, devices 15, critical_care 14. 21 audit-like tables exist in the ORM, 12 built, but only audit_logs carries the chain.
findings.affected_components: app/ (25 packages); canonical chain in app/services/audit_service.py
findings.affected_users: Anyone relying on the audit trail to reconstruct who changed what
findings.clinical_impact: blood_bank (21 unaudited mutating endpoints) and critical_care (14) are traceability domains: blood product lifecycle and infusion changes are exactly what an audit trail exists to reconstruct.
findings.security_impact: An audit trail with a 22% floor of unaudited mutations cannot answer 'who changed this', and the hash chain's tamper-evidence applies only to what was written to it.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Mutations outside the chain are unreconstructable after the fact.
findings.operational_impact: Incident reconstruction and compliance evidence are incomplete by an unknown margin.
findings.scalability_impact: Session-level enforcement would add one insert per audited mutation; the chain is already serialized on last-hash read.
findings.legal_impact: ISO 27001 A.8.15 is cited in the audit service docstring; partial coverage weakens that claim.
findings.dependencies: NR-045 (canonical audit write repair, VERIFIED), NR-060 (consent audits all five decision branches).
findings.intersections: NR-045, NR-060, NR-021. NR-065 (the package blind spot this now measures around: app/national counts as auditing because interop.py does, while task_engine and workflow_runtime contain no audit call). NR-066 (what app/governance writes instead).
findings.contradictions: CLAUDE.md security invariant #2 states all mutations MUST write to the audit log; measurement shows at least 22% do not.
findings.recommended_fix: ENFORCE AT THE SESSION, NOT THE ROUTE. The mutation classes that must produce audit evidence are: clinical result/order state changes; authorization decisions including break-glass; identity lifecycle and role assignment; consent grant/revoke; blood product and controlled-substance lifecycle; financial and billing mutations; tenant/scope changes; and bulk export or disclosure of patient data. Enforcing per route has failed for 271 endpoints because it depends on an author remembering. A SQLAlchemy before_flush hook over a declared set of audit-worthy tables cannot be forgotten, sees the actual INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, and can reuse infrastructure that already exists: database.py maintains per-request contextvars (request_id, endpoint, user_id, lab_id) for error correlation, which is exactly the actor context an audit row needs. NOT implemented here -- it changes write behaviour on every session and needs its own review.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED, additive only: backend/tests/test_audit_chain_invariant.py ratchets the measured gap. Each declared package may shed unaudited mutations; none may gain them, no new unaudited package may appear, and a resolved entry must be removed rather than left as a stale allowance. The chain's own integrity (chain hash, previous-hash link, HMAC anchor, verifier) is asserted too, because the invariant is only worth enforcing while the chain is real. No runtime code changed.
findings.verification_method: 7 tests. Package ratchet (declared per-package counts, no new package, no stale entry), chain-integrity assertion, and a module-level aggregate ratchet. Negative-proven by removing app/governance from the ledger -- the guard fails naming it, proving the detector correction is load-bearing -- and by adding an unaudited mutating module, which fails the module ratchet with '131 modules ... up from 130'. Both restored byte-identical.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Every mutation class listed above produces a hash-chained audit entry, enforced where it cannot be forgotten.
findings.regression_risk: None from this change; tests only. The recommended session hook carries real risk and is deliberately not applied.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG for the lower bound (AST over the whole route surface); the upper bound is explicitly a proxy

findings.title: 103 create paths splat an unvalidated request body into an ORM constructor; 75 set no tenant or actor
findings.description: Found while trying to resolve NR-022's nine REVIEW sites. They could not be decided from their call sites, and the reason mattered more than the question: the call sites are generic passthroughs. A route takes a bare `data: dict` with no request model and hands it to `Model(**data)`. Measured across app/: 103 such constructions. 28 set tenant and/or actor server-side; 75 set neither, so the request body would decide every column including lab_id, verified_by and is_deleted. PHASE G CLASSIFICATION, against the running application: LIVE 0, REACHABLE-BUT-INACTIVE 75, DEAD 0, UNKNOWN 0. All three modules (care_continuum_service 40, clinical_service 18, ehr_service 17) are a DIRECT import of a registered route module -- exactly NR-064's shape, where the route was clean and its service was not. So the only thing between these paths and a live mass-assignment surface is the absent table, which NR-022 and NR-059 both propose to create. A first pass classified ehr_service's 17 as DEAD and was wrong: app/routes/ehr.py:29 imports it through the package form the resolver could not see (NR-079). 'Dead' is the answer an undercounting instrument gives, and the most comfortable one to be wrong about.
findings.root_cause: Create paths were written as untyped dict passthroughs, so neither validation nor server-side tenancy has anywhere to live.
findings.evidence: AST scan for `Model(**param)` where param is a function argument, cross-referenced against the migration-derived built-table set. 103 sites; unguarded concentrated in care_continuum_service (40), clinical_service (18), ehr_service (17). The defensible pattern is `ClinicalTask(lab_id=lab_id, created_by=user_id, assigned_by=user_id, **data)` -- tenant and actor come from the authenticated user, a colliding body key raises TypeError rather than overriding, and those paths audit. CRITICAL SAFETY FACT: zero of the 75 unguarded sites targets a built table, so every such write currently fails with UndefinedTable before a row exists. The pattern is latent, not live. Detector note: server-setting occurs in two forms -- an explicit keyword and a pre-splat `data['key'] = value` mutation. The first version of this scan counted only the former and reported create_compliance_check as unguarded when it does set the actor by mutation; corrected before shipping, which moved the split from 27/76 to 28/75. RE-MEASURED with import-resolved model names (absolute, relative and package re-exports): 104 splat constructions, of which 103 are ORM models (GatewayMessage in app/integration is a plain class), 28 guarded, 75 unguarded, and **zero unguarded targeting a built table** -- the original figures confirmed exactly. They were, however, produced by a bare class-name lookup, which is unsound here: ComplianceCheck alone names three tables. The conclusion was right by coincidence rather than by method, so the guard now resolves through tests/orm_resolution.py.

findings.title: National orchestration tenancy is undecided; laboratory scope is now eliminated, and the untenanted surface is 84 of 113 national tables, not 15
findings.description: NR-059 left activation blocked on product intent. Unit 3 ran the checks the approved decision actually gates on and found two more blockers that do not depend on that question. All 15 task and workflow tables extend `BaseEntity` -- the one national base carrying neither TenantMixin nor AuditMixin, while TenantEntity, AuditEntity and TenantAuditEntity all exist alongside it. Only national_workflow_executions has a tenant column. The task listing path filters on status, priority, category, assignee, queue_id and a title LIKE, and on nothing else, because there is nothing else to filter on. Neither package contains a call reaching the hash-chained audit log, and there is no idempotency key or row lock anywhere in a package containing a saga engine and a workflow state machine. SHARPENED: the earlier reading of '1 of 15 tenanted' was too generous. `tenant_id` appears in exactly six places across both packages -- the column, a domain-entity field defaulting to None, a service parameter defaulting to None, the pass-through to the model and two serialisation points -- and NO route supplies it. The routes derive created_by from current_user.id and stop. So the column is written NULL on every path that could write it, and the surface is untenanted with one column that looks like tenancy and is not. UNIT 7 (platform-wide evidence): the earlier verdict listed four candidates and chose none, but it was reached from inside task_engine and workflow_runtime alone. RoleScopeType and MembershipScopeType -- the two vocabularies that decide what a role or membership may be scoped to -- are organization|facility|department|unit|workspace. Neither has a lab member or a governorate member, so a national artifact keyed by lab_id could not be named by any role assignment: nothing could be granted over it and nothing denied. The vocabulary is enforced rather than declared (MembershipService._validate_context raises 'Unsupported membership scope' on a miss; AuthorizationServiceV2 takes scope_type from the role, never from the caller) and every table behind it is built. niam_role_assignments.organization_id is nullable=False with facility/department/unit/workspace as nullable narrowings, all ULID String(26) into niam_* -- where TenantMixin.lab_id is an INTEGER into labs.id, so the laboratory option is also a type-level mismatch. TenantMixin is therefore eliminated, and governorate is eliminated as a *scope* because there is no governorate entity to point at: niam_organizations.governorate is a nullable String(50) attribute of an organization, not a level above or below one. Remaining question, still reserved: organization root, or genuinely national and deliberately unscoped. findings.status: MEASURED — latent, not live; no partner authentication path exists to be bypassed
findings.title: The external-partner credential subsystem is a registry with no enforcement path, and its non-API-key comparison branch is plaintext and non-constant-time
findings.description: app/national/ecosystem ships six BUILT tables (ecosystem_partners, _partner_credentials, _partner_certificates, _partner_rate_limits, _partner_audit_logs, _partner_agreements) and is registered in factory.py (ecosystem_router, ecosystem_gateway_router). Two gaps. (1) CredentialManager.validate_credential (partners/service.py:187) has ZERO callers anywhere in app/ -- partner credential validation is never performed, so registering a partner credential grants and denies nothing. (2) Inside it, credential_type == 'api_key' hashes the presented value and compares with hmac.compare_digest (correct), but every other credential_type falls through to `credential.credential_value != credential_value` -- a plaintext, non-constant-time comparison against a stored value. That branch is unreachable today because issue_api_key is the only issuer and always stores a sha3_512 HMAC under credential_type='api_key'; the first non-api-key issuer makes it live. The gateway alongside it is not an enforcement point either: GatewayPolicyEngine keeps its policies and routes in plain in-process dicts (per-worker, not persisted), the router is guarded by require_permission('system:admin'), and nothing outside app/national/ecosystem references the engine. It evaluates a dict an admin supplies; it does not sit on any request path. So no partner traffic is authenticated anywhere, which is why (1) has caused no incident and why (2) has never executed. This is recorded as latent, NOT as a live vulnerability.
findings.root_cause: The ecosystem package was built as a data model plus an admin-facing API without the runtime that would consume it: no ingress path resolves a partner, so the credential check has no caller and the policy engine has no traffic.
findings.evidence: grep for 'validate_credential' across backend/ returns exactly one hit, its own definition (app/national/ecosystem/partners/service.py:187). grep for GatewayPolicyEngine / PartnerService / CredentialManager outside app/national/ecosystem returns nothing. policies.py:366-369 GatewayPolicyEngine.__init__ stores dict[str, BasePolicy] and dict[str, dict]. gateway/routes.py:13-17 router dependencies=[Depends(require_permission('system:admin'))]. partners/service.py:219 _hash_api_key = hmac.new(SECRET_KEY, api_key, hashlib.sha3_512); the api_key branch uses hmac.compare_digest, the else branch uses `!=`.
findings.affected_users: None today (no partner ingress path exists); external integration partners once one does
findings.clinical_impact: None currently — no clinical data flows through the ecosystem gateway
findings.security_impact: LATENT. If a non-api_key credential type is ever issued, secrets would be stored in plaintext and compared non-constant-time, exposing them to timing analysis and to any read of ecosystem_partner_credentials. Separately, a future ingress path that assumes validate_credential is wired would authenticate nobody.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — no writes are gated on the unreachable check
findings.operational_impact: Six built tables carry state that changes no behaviour; operators may read the registry as enforcement
findings.legal_impact: A partner agreement row implies a governed integration that is not in fact governed at runtime

findings.title: Both registered orchestration routers perform no authorization at all, update_task assigns from the request body, and the assignment actor is client-supplied
findings.description: Found by the NR-065 Unit 8 caller trace. factory.py:695 and :698 register workflow_runtime and task_engine, and NEITHER route module contains a single require_permission -- not at the router, not on any handler. Every endpoint depends on get_current_user alone. That covers create/list/execute/cancel/pause/resume/approve/reject for workflows and create/bulk/assign/start/complete/fail/cancel/escalate/delegate/delete for tasks, plus unfiltered list endpoints. Any authenticated principal -- including a laboratory technician with no national role -- would have full control of the national orchestration surface. Two further shapes on the same paths: (1) TaskEngineService.update_task does `for key, value in updates.items(): if hasattr(task, key) and key not in ('id','created_at','version'): setattr(task, key, value)`, so created_by, assigned_to, assigned_by, status and correlation_id are all client-writable -- the actor fields an audit trail relies on, and a bypass of the state machine the transition methods enforce; (2) POST /{task_id}/assign takes data.get('assigned_by') and POST /{task_id}/escalate takes data.get('escalated_to') from the body while current_user is resolved on the same handler and used for created_by. LATENT for exactly one reason: none of the fifteen tables is built, so every path raises UndefinedTable before it can act. This is the blocker that must clear before NR-065's scope columns are written -- a correct organization_id behind an unauthorized endpoint is a correctly-labelled open door. FIXED. All three shapes closed in one change. (1) AUTHORIZATION: the two orchestration routers now carry `dependencies=[Depends(require_permission("system:admin"))]` at the router. findings.status: PARTIALLY VERIFIED — autogenerate now executes inside a CI gate; the topology change is DECIDED (Option A) and deliberately NOT APPLIED, because applying it would make a 1379-operation destructive diff actionable (NR-080)
findings.title: 310 foreign keys name a table their own declarative base does not own, and as a result `alembic revision --autogenerate` cannot run against this repository at all
findings.description: NR-075 generalised, and it turns out to be a defect in the measuring instrument rather than in one endpoint. SQLAlchemy resolves a ForeignKey inside the MetaData that owns the REFERRING table. Measured across exactly what `migrations/env.py` hands Alembic, 310 foreign keys point at a table owned by a different declarative base: CareContinuumBase 214, EHRBase 70, DataPlatformBase 13, TrustBase 8, IdentityBase 5. The targets are real tables -- national_practitioners (78), national_patients (51), national_citizens (50), national_facilities (49), national_encounters (30) and 18 more -- owned by NationalBase and Base. CONSEQUENCE: Alembic reaches `MetaData.sorted_tables` on every registered metadata before it emits a single operation, and sorting resolves every foreign key. So `alembic revision --autogenerate -m "anything"` terminates with NoReferencedTableError and produces nothing. That is the command CLAUDE.md's migration policy names as the way to make any schema change ('All schema changes = new revision: alembic revision --autogenerate'), and it has no working path. WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT: `test_alembic_metadata_registry.py` asks whether a foreign key names a table that exists SOMEWHERE across the registry -- PHANTOM_FK_TARGETS, currently empty -- which is one qualifier weaker than what SQLAlchemy requires. Every guard in that file reasons about what autogenerate WOULD propose, and not one of them has ever asked autogenerate to propose it. The capability was assumed by the guards that depend on it and exercised by none of them. EXPERIMENTAL RESOLUTION. Both options were measured against a disposable PostgreSQL 16.13 database migrated to head, rather than argued. OPTION B (keep separate metadata, drop the ORM-level ForeignKey, keep columns and physical constraints) removes nothing the ORM uses: NOT ONE of the 76 tables holding a cross-base FK carries a single relationship(), so there is no navigation to lose. It clears all 310 -- and then fails on a second, independent blocker: 'ValueError: Duplicate table keys across multiple MetaData objects: national_facilities'. Alembic refuses a multi-metadata target claiming one table twice, and NR-006's repair deliberately declares national_facilities a second time as a FOREIGN-KEY ANCHOR so seventeen app/national models can resolve it. The anchor is what makes those FKs work and what makes autogenerate refuse. Option B cannot hold both goals. OPTION A (one shared MetaData) was measured: exactly ONE duplicate table key -- that same anchor -- and the two definitions are COLUMN-IDENTICAL, so the collision is resolved by deleting one declaration rather than by choosing an owner; ZERO unresolved foreign keys; sorted_tables succeeds; autogenerate runs. Option A is the mechanically correct topology and the repository is one deleted Table away from it. IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT APPLIED. Making autogenerate run is not the same as making it usable: the resulting diff is 5060 operations of which 1379 are destructive, including DROP COLUMN on patients.national_id -- the column Security Invariant #8 requires to hold encrypted national identifiers (NR-080). Applying Option A today would replace a loud, honest failure ('autogenerate cannot run') with a quiet and dangerous capability ('autogenerate runs and proposes dropping your encrypted national IDs'). That is the same trade NR-076 refuses, in the same direction. THIS CORRECTS THIS FINDING'S OWN EARLIER FRAMING, which presented the topology choice as the decision to take: the topology is not the bottleneck, the drift is. WHAT IS APPLIED: backend/tests/test_autogenerate_is_safe.py performs the merge inside the gate, so autogenerate executes for real against a migrated PostgreSQL without migrations/env.py, any declarative base or any model changing -- zero runtime risk -- and pins every destructive proposal with its explanation.
findings.root_cause: Domain packages were given their own declarative bases (NR-018 registered eight authorized ones) while their models kept declaring foreign keys to the shared national and legacy tables. The physical constraints exist because migrations create them by name; the ORM cannot see the targets.
findings.evidence: Executed: `alembic revision --autogenerate -m nr075_probe` against the migrated PostgreSQL 16.13 database (nr069_truth) fails with "NoReferencedTableError: Foreign key associated with column 'ehr_allergies.citizen_id' could not find table 'national_citizens'" and writes no revision file. `alembic.autogenerate.produce_migrations` fails at the same point, inside alembic/autogenerate/api.py::sorted_tables. Static: iterating the labelled target_metadata the checked-in harness loads from env.py and counting foreign keys whose `_table_key()` is absent from the referring table's own MetaData gives 310, distributed over the five bases above. Negative proofs, both restored byte-identical: removing one FK from CitizenRelationship fails the rot check with 'IdentityBase (5, 4)'; adding a cross-base FK to a PharmacyBase model fails the ratchet with "['PharmacyBase']". | EXPERIMENTAL EVIDENCE (disposable database nr078_probe, PostgreSQL 16.13, 423 tables at head): baseline autogenerate CRASHES with NoReferencedTableError on ehr_allergies. Option B removes 310 of 310 cross-base FK constraints from the metadata (leftover 0) and then CRASHES with ValueError duplicate table key national_facilities. Option A: 1 collision (national_facilities, identical_columns=true), 0 unresolved FKs, sorted_tables OK, autogenerate produces 5060 operations. Runtime relationship census: 218 relationships across 18 SQLAlchemy registries, of which 0 are on any of the 76 cross-base-FK tables. Physical cross-check: only 12 of the 310 cross-base FKs have an actual PostgreSQL constraint, and 70 of the 76 referring tables are not physical at all. The 12 that are real sit on trust_* (8), niam_assignments (2) and niam_citizen_relationships (2). Gate: 7 tests, 4 negative proofs, all sources restored byte-identical.

findings.title: Reachability was measured by regex over factory.py and an import resolver blind to `from package import submodule`, understating the reachable surface by 63 route modules and 382 modules of closure
findings.description: Found while executing PHASE G -- classifying NR-063's 75 latent create paths as LIVE / REACHABLE-BUT-INACTIVE / REGISTERED-FUTURE / DEAD / UNKNOWN before fixing any of them. The first classification returned 17 DEAD, which was false, and the falseness had two independent causes, both understating reachability: (1) REGISTRATION BY REGEX. `_registered_route_modules()` matched `from .x import y as z` and `from .routes import name as alias` in factory.py. The factory also registers a bulk block -- `from .routes import (admin, ehr, ehr_fhir, …)` followed by `for r in core_routes + feature_routes + advanced_routes + …: app.include_router(r.router)` -- which neither regex matched. Measured against the running application the regex finds 79 route modules where 142 are served: 63 false negatives, 0 false positives. (2) SUBMODULE IMPORTS DROPPED. `_imported_modules()` resolved `from app.x.y import Z` and `from ..models import Z` but turned `from app.services import ehr_service` into a lookup for app/services.py, which does not exist, instead of app/services/ehr_service.py, which does. That single form hid an entire module holding 17 unguarded create paths and 63 reachable reads of unbuilt tables. Plain `import app.x.y` was also unhandled. Together the two took the reachable closure from 612 modules to 994 (+62%) and NR-067's reachable unbuilt reads from 418 across 20 route modules to 610 across 24. The guard-the-guard that should have caught it asserted at least 60 registered modules -- satisfied comfortably by an instrument missing 63. A floor is only worth its distance from the truth.

findings.title: The first complete comparison of the ORM against the database proposes 5060 operations, 1379 of them destructive, including DROP COLUMN on patients.national_id
findings.description: NR-078 established that `alembic revision --autogenerate` has never run against this repository. Making it run (Option A, inside a gate) produced the first complete ORM-to-database comparison the platform has ever had, and it is not small: 5060 operations, of which 538 DropConstraintOp, 454 DropIndexOp, 377 DropColumnOp and 10 DropTableOp -- 1379 destructive. None of it is caused by the topology change; the topology change only made pre-existing drift visible. TWO SAMPLES DECIDE HOW SERIOUS IT IS. (1) The 10 proposed DROP TABLE are EXACTLY the ten physical tables no ORM maps, independently pinned as UNMAPPED_PHYSICAL_TABLES in test_alembic_metadata_registry.py by subtracting mapped from physical -- a completely different derivation reaching the same list, which is strong evidence both instruments are correct. They are Financial Engine Phase A (schema-only by design), visits, sndhs_audit_logs, idempotency_keys and radiology_ai_analysis_jobs. (2) The proposed DROP COLUMN set includes patients.national_id, patients.sndhs_health_id, patients.identity_level, patients.consent_flags and lab_orders.visit_id -- the SNDHS Phase 1 surface. patients.national_id is varchar(20), carries four indexes including a partial unique index, and is the column CLAUDE.md Security Invariant #8 requires to hold encrypted national identifiers. app/models/patient.py maps national_id_hash and none of the others. CONSEQUENCE: autogenerate output may not be committed as a migration in this repository under any topology until this is reconciled. That is why NR-078's topology change is decided but not applied -- the capability is worth less than the hazard until the drift comes down. The largest single cluster is radiology (~170 columns across 12 tables), which is the NR-074 class at scale.

findings.evidence: Disposable PostgreSQL 16.13 (nr078_probe) migrated to head, 423 tables. alembic.autogenerate.produce_migrations against the merged metadata: CreateIndexOp 2372, ModifyTableOps 585, DropConstraintOp 538, DropIndexOp 454, DropColumnOp 377, AddColumnOp 314, CreateTableOp 303, AlterColumnOp 73, CreateForeignKeyOp 27, DropTableOp 10, CreateUniqueConstraintOp 7. findings.title: Schema access through `sqlalchemy.table()` and raw SQL is invisible to every metadata-based guard, and one unreachable subsystem writes three canonical clinical tables that way
findings.description: Found while tracing NR-080's discovery that patients.national_id is physical, indexed four ways and mapped by no ORM model. Something does read it: app/reference/infrastructure/repositories.py, through `_PATIENTS = table('patients', column(...), ...)` -- the lightweight SQLAlchemy Core construct, which carries NO MetaData at all -- plus raw `INSERT INTO patients`, returning national_id in its response shape. Every schema instrument in this suite works from ORM metadata: built_tables() derives from migrations, the registry guard compares registered MetaData against PostgreSQL, the autogenerate gate diffs mappers against the database, and the NR-063/NR-067 scans resolve ORM class names. NONE of them can see a `table()` construct or a table name inside a string literal. This is a whole class of schema access that was structurally invisible. MEASURED: 1 module reaches a built table through a Core table() construct, and 7 execute raw INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE against one. Six of the seven are legitimate and stay -- the three AI modules write their own tables, idempotency_keys has no ORM by design, outbox_events needs raw SQL for its locking, and startup_guard seeds lab_users before the app is up. Legitimacy is not the invariant; visibility is. THE OUTLIER: app/reference is a complete parallel implementation of patient reference data -- own domain model, own repository, own tests -- which writes patients, lab_orders and lab_results by raw SQL. Measured against the running application it serves ZERO routes and ZERO modules outside it import it, so it is unreachable today. It is recorded rather than deleted: removing a subsystem is an ownership decision. If it were ever registered there would be a second write authority for the clinical subject, with different invariants and no HMAC path for the national ID, and no existing guard would have noticed.

findings.title: Radiology is a registered clinical module serving 50 HTTP paths in which no database operation of any kind can succeed: all 18 mappers are a second generation that never replaced the first
findings.description: Every one of the 18 SQLAlchemy classes on RadiologyBase fails to execute even a plain SELECT against a database at migration head. Executed, not inferred: `SELECT <mapper columns> FROM <table> LIMIT 1` was run against a disposable PostgreSQL 16 migrated to head for all 18, and 18 failed — 17 with UndefinedColumn and `radiology_ai_jobs` with UndefinedTable, because no migration builds that name (the physical table is `radiology_ai_analysis_jobs`, and the two share 16 of their column names). INSERT fails identically. app/radiology/routes.py is registered in factory.py and serves 50 paths over app/radiology/services.py, which uses these mappers directly, so the module is reachable and totally non-functional. The routes carry no broad exception handler, so the failure surfaces as a 500 rather than as a valid-looking empty response.
findings.root_cause: Two generations of the radiology domain share table names and were never reconciled. The physical tables are Generation A: integer primary keys, joined to the platform core (patient_id -> patients.id, lab_id -> labs.id, *_by -> lab_users.id), carrying lab_id, sync_id, created_by and updated_by. The mappers are Generation B: String(26) ULID keys, FHIR-flavoured, with no foreign key to the core and no lab_id at all. All 18 primary keys disagree on type. This is the same pattern already resolved for pharmacy, where the 17 Generation-B mappers were rewritten from the physical schema.
findings.evidence: 494 physical columns across 18 tables vs 399 mapper columns; 265 physical-only and 170 mapper-only. Systematic physical-only columns: sync_id 17/17, lab_id 13/17, created_by 12/17, updated_by 10/17. Systematic mapper-only: extra_metadata 17/17. 45 columns present in both disagree on type, including all 18 primary keys (String(26) vs integer) and radiology_protocols.version (Integer lock vs character varying). Runtime probe: SELECT ok=0 fail=18; INSERT UndefinedColumn on radiology_orders(encounter_id), radiology_exams(exam_code), radiology_reports(ordering_provider_id), UndefinedTable on radiology_ai_jobs. Route probe: route_modules(app) contains app/radiology/routes.py and 50 served paths resolve to it. API-CONTRACT AND CLIENT EVIDENCE (added; this is what the blocked decision needs): the response models in app/radiology/routes.py declare every identifier as Pydantic `str` (patient_id, order_id, exam_id, protocol_id, technologist_id...), over physical columns that are `integer`. NO CLIENT CONSUMES THEM: across all four frontends (frontend-v3, frontend-v2, client, frontend) there is not one call to a /radiology backend path. The only three frontend-v3 files mentioning radiology are api/generated/types.ts (generated declarations, not calls), pages/migration/frontendSurfaceCatalog.ts (a UI entryPath '/radiology'), and a legacy route-bridge test. And the decisive argument does not depend on searching this repository: every one of the 18 mappers fails on SELECT, so no endpoint backed by them has ever returned a row, and an endpoint that has never returned a row cannot have a dependent client inside or outside this repository.
findings.affected_users: Any actor reaching a /radiology path; radiologists, technologists, referring clinicians, citizens using the image-share endpoints.
findings.clinical_impact: Total. Orders, exams, reports, critical findings, worklists and DICOM references cannot be created or read. radiology_critical_findings is the escalation path for findings that require immediate clinician contact and it does not work.
findings.security_impact: CLAUDE.md Security Invariant #1 requires every patient-data query to filter on lab_id = current_user.lab_id. The physical tables carry lab_id with a foreign key to labs; the mappers do not declare it, so no ORM query in this domain can filter by tenant. If the mappers were repaired without adding lab_id, the module would become functional and cross-tenant in the same change. That is the trap this finding exists to prevent.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Nothing is currently corrupted, because nothing is currently written. The risk is in the repair: autogenerate proposes DROP for the 265 physical-only columns, which includes every lab_id, created_by, updated_by and sync_id in the domain.
findings.operational_impact: 50 registered endpoints return 500 on every database-touching call.
findings.scalability_impact: None measured; the module does no work.
findings.legal_impact: Radiology reports and critical findings are part of the clinical record; an unwritable record is a records-retention gap.
findings.contradictions: docs and CLAUDE.md describe app/radiology/ as a platform sub-package alongside pharmacy and nursing, which are reconciled and working. Nothing distinguishes radiology as non-functional.
findings.recommended_fix: Rewrite the 18 mappers from the physical schema, as was done for pharmacy — and note the response models must be reshaped in the same change, which is free because nothing consumes them: integer keys, lab_id with its ForeignKey('labs.id'), created_by/updated_by to lab_users, sync_id; then reconcile services.py and routes.py field references; then add a migration for the Generation-B fields that carry information the physical schema genuinely lacks. Map radiology_ai_jobs onto radiology_ai_analysis_jobs. Enforce lab_id filtering in services.py before re-enabling.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: None that makes the module work. Partial repair is worse than none here: a mapper fixed for readability but still missing lab_id turns a dead endpoint into a cross-tenant one. The safe increment already applied is measurement — NR-083's guard pins all 17 readable failures so the repair cannot silently regress or half-land.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_mapped_tables_are_readable.py executes each mapper's own SELECT against PostgreSQL in the migration CI job; the 17 radiology entries must leave DECLARED_UNREADABLE as they are repaired, and the rot check fails if a repaired table is left in the ledger.
findings.acceptance_criteria: All 18 radiology mappers read and write against a database at head; every mapper declares lab_id; every service query filters on it; the 17 radiology entries are gone from DECLARED_UNREADABLE; no physical column was dropped to achieve it.

findings.blocker: Narrowed. The API-compatibility half is ANSWERED: no client depends on these contracts, so the mappers can adopt the physical integer keys and the response models can be reshaped without breaking anyone — the same situation as the seven M4 pharmacy response models. findings.title: 35 mapped tables that exist in PostgreSQL cannot be read by the mapper that claims them, and no guard had ever asked a mapper to run its own query
findings.description: Every schema guard in this suite compared descriptions of the schema — metadata against metadata, migration against model, list against list. Doing so for all 715 registered tables found that 303 have no physical table (independently equal to the autogenerate gate's CreateTableOp count of 303) and that of the 412 that do exist, 44 name at least one column their table does not have. Existing guards proved that migrations apply, that metadata is registered and that tables exist — none of which is disturbed by a mapper naming a column that is not there. The condition is invisible to `alembic upgrade head`, to table-existence checks and to the SQLite-backed unit suite, and visible only to PostgreSQL at statement time.

findings.status: PARTLY REPAIRED — 9 of 19 columns fixed and regression-guarded; 10 pinned. SEVERITY RAISED P2 -> P1 by execution: the enum group was first recorded as latent, and it was not
findings.title: 19 columns in readable tables disagree with their PostgreSQL type — and for nine of them the column's own server_default was unreadable by the model that owns it
findings.description: NR-083 asks whether a mapper can read its table, which only checks that column NAMES line up. It says nothing about Column(Integer) over a character varying. Measuring that found 19 columns across 15 otherwise-readable tables, in three groups. (1) Six blood-bank tables inherit AuditMixin.created_by as Integer over a varchar column — the seventh, blood_bank_transfusions, was built with an integer column and agrees, so the migrations disagree with each other. (2) Four Integer mappers over boolean columns, including oauth2_tokens.is_revoked. (3) Nine trust_* native-enum mappers over plain varchar — REPAIRED here.
findings.root_cause: For groups 1 and 2, columns were added by migrations written against a different type than the mapper declares, and nothing compared the two. For group 3 the cause is sharper and systemic: SQLAlchemy persists an enum member's NAME unless values_callable says otherwise, and none of the seven trust enum classes passed it — while every migration wrote its server_default as the member's VALUE. All seven classes are UPPER_SNAKE name / lower_snake value, so the two halves of one intent disagreed on all nine columns. The database has no native enum types at all, so the mappers also compiled to a PostgreSQL type that does not exist.
findings.evidence: Executed against PostgreSQL 16 at head. Groups 1-2: INSERT into blood_bank_reservations with created_by as both str '7' and int 7 succeeded and the route passes str(current_user.id), so writes work; `WHERE created_by = 42` -> UndefinedFunction: operator does not exist: character varying = integer; `WHERE is_revoked = 1` -> boolean = integer (while `= True` compiles to IS true). Group 3, the part first reported as latent and proven otherwise: an INSERT omitting trust_consent_records.status takes the DATABASE's own default 'pending', and reading that row through the mapper raised LookupError; a plain SELECT * over the table then raised for EVERY row; and `WHERE status == 'PENDING'` matched 1 of 2 semantically-pending rows — an undercount rather than an error. 13 routes under /api/v1/trust/* are registered and served over these tables. After the repair, the same probe reads the default row, reads a legacy name-spelled row, and `status == ConsentStatus.PENDING` matches 2 of 2. CORRECTION (NR-086): the statement that the trust routes are 'registered and served over these tables' implied those writes worked. They do not. Every proof above used Core select() and raw SQL, which never trigger SQLAlchemy's table sorting; a real Session + model instance + flush raises NoReferencedTableError on four of the six trust tables, because their foreign keys target another MetaData. The enum repair is still correct and still necessary — it fixes reads and the server_default, proven by reading a real row back as <ConsentStatus.GRANTED: 'granted'> — but the trust write path remains broken for a different reason, recorded as NR-086.
findings.affected_users: None today. The exposure is to the next person who writes a filter.
findings.clinical_impact: None measured. The blood-bank write path works because the route passes a string.
findings.security_impact: oauth2_tokens.is_revoked is the column deciding whether a token has been revoked; a check written as `is_revoked == 1` raises rather than answering wrongly, so it fails closed, but it is one keystroke from an outage in the revocation path. For the trust group the exposure was consent and data-sovereignty records: trust_consent_records.status and trust_sovereignty_rules.sovereignty_level both had a server_default their mapper could not read.
findings.data_integrity_impact: The trust group could not corrupt a value, but it could make one unreadable and could silently undercount a filtered query — the more dangerous of the two. Repaired. The remaining ten are comparison-time hazards with no current wrong answer.
findings.operational_impact: None today.
findings.legal_impact: trust_consent_records.status and trust_sovereignty_rules.sovereignty_level are consent and data-residency records.
findings.contradictions: Six of seven sibling audit tables disagree with the mixin they share; the seventh agrees. Nothing documents which is intended.
findings.recommended_fix: Group 3 applied: app/trust/models.py::_enum declares native_enum=False (compiling to the VARCHAR the column actually is) plus values_callable (persisting and reading the value the migrations already default to), and migration 20260915_0003 brings any row written in the name spelling across. Groups 1-2 still need a decision rather than a patch: is the audit actor an integer lab_users.id or an opaque string, and should the four Integer-over-boolean mappers become Boolean.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: The enum repair is mapper-side plus a corrective UPDATE bounded to the exact enum names. Nothing is dropped, renamed, retyped or truncated, and a value that is neither a name nor a value is left exactly as it is rather than coerced — it is then reported by the guard instead of being silently rewritten. Reversible: downgrade performs the inverse mapping, bounded the same way.
findings.verification_method: Two layers in the migration CI job. test_mapped_tables_are_readable.py ratchets the type-conflict ledger (the nine are removed, so reverting reintroduces them as undeclared conflicts). test_enum_defaults_are_readable.py asserts the invariant directly and generally: the database has no native enum types, every enum mapper compiles to VARCHAR, and every enum column's own server_default is readable by its mapper — which also covers the 33 enum columns on tables still in NR-083's unreadable ledger, so radiology and NHDW cannot reintroduce the split. Two negative proofs: reverting to bare Enum fails both files; keeping native_enum=False but dropping values_callable passes the type check and still fails default-readability, proving the two halves are independently guarded.
findings.acceptance_criteria: DECLARED_TYPE_CONFLICTS is empty and DECLARED_UNREADABLE_DEFAULTS stays empty, with each remaining group resolved by an explicit decision.
findings.regression_risk: Low. The enum change is mapper-side; the migration is corrective, bounded and reversible; round trip executed. A deployment holding values outside the enum keeps them and is reported rather than rewritten.

findings.domain: platform-wide ORM write path; live instance in app/trust
findings.status: MEASURED AND GUARDED — 76 tables pinned and ratcheted; the topology repair that empties it is NR-078
findings.title: 76 mapped tables cannot be written through the ORM at all: their foreign keys target another MetaData, so every INSERT and UPDATE raises before emitting SQL
findings.description: SQLAlchemy resolves every ForeignKey target while sorting a mapper's tables during flush. A target in a different MetaData cannot be found, so the write raises NoReferencedTableError before any SQL is emitted. Reads are unaffected, which is exactly why this hides: SELECT never sorts tables, so the table looks healthy to the readability guard (NR-083), to every migration check, and to any route that only lists. Asking which mappers resolve every target inside their own MetaData gives 76 tables carrying 310 unresolvable foreign keys: CareContinuumBase 45, EHRBase 16, DataPlatformBase 9, TrustBase 4, IdentityBase 2.
findings.root_cause: The same declarative-base topology NR-078 documents. NR-078 measured 310 cross-base foreign keys across 76 tables and recorded them as a TOPOLOGY problem — the thing that stops alembic autogenerate running. They are also 76 tables no ORM write can reach, and that consequence had not been stated. NR-075 recorded one instance (niam_citizen_relationships) as a runtime write failure without connecting it to the population.
findings.evidence: Executed: Session + real model instance + flush against PostgreSQL 16 at head. session.add(ConsentRecord(...)); session.flush() -> NoReferencedTableError: Foreign key associated with column 'trust_consent_records.guardian_id' could not find table 'lab_users'. The ORM UPDATE path fails identically: loading an existing row succeeds and returns <ConsentStatus.GRANTED: 'granted'>, then mutating and flushing raises. Operation matrix over the trust base: trust_consent_records, trust_service_logs, trust_compliance_checks and trust_compliance_evidence all give ORM SELECT OK / ORM INSERT NoReferencedTableError; trust_sovereignty_rules, which carries no cross-base FK, gives OK / OK. Platform-wide count 76 tables / 310 FKs is independently equal to NR-078's separately measured cross-base FK population — two derivations, one by Alembic topology and one by asking each mapper to resolve its own targets, agreeing exactly.
findings.affected_users: Any actor calling a write endpoint backed by one of the 76 tables.
findings.clinical_impact: The live instance is the trust platform: app/trust/routes.py serves 13 registered paths of which SIX are writes — POST /api/v1/trust/consent, /consent/{id}/withdraw, /sign, /timestamp, /compliance/check, /compliance/evidence. All six land on the four trust tables carrying a cross-base FK, and all six fail. Consent capture and consent withdrawal are among them. The wider 76 include the care-continuum and EHR bases.
findings.security_impact: Consent withdrawal cannot be recorded. A platform that cannot persist a withdrawal has no mechanism to honour it, and the failure is a 500 rather than a refusal, so nothing downstream learns the withdrawal was not stored.
findings.data_integrity_impact: No corruption: the write raises before SQL is emitted, so nothing partial is persisted. The integrity risk is the absence of records that callers believe they created.
findings.operational_impact: Six registered trust endpoints return 500 on every call; the same holds for any write endpoint backed by the other 72 tables.
findings.legal_impact: Consent records and their withdrawal are a legal control under any health-data regime.
findings.contradictions: My own NR-085 commit message stated that thirteen trust routes are 'registered and served over these tables, including consent creation and withdrawal', which implied they worked. They do not, and never have. Every NR-085 proof used Core select() and raw SQL, which never trigger table sorting. Corrected here rather than left standing.
findings.recommended_fix: This is NR-078's repair, not a separate one. Option A (one shared MetaData) resolves all 310 at once, and NR-078 has already measured that NOT ONE of these 76 tables carries a relationship(), so no ORM navigation is lost either way. The alternative — replacing each cross-base ForeignKey with the plain column it should be — is equally available and equally safe for the same reason. Neither may be applied before the NR-080 drift is reconciled, because Option A also makes autogenerate propose dropping patients.national_id.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: None that is safe today, and that is the finding rather than a gap in it. The increment applied is measurement: backend/tests/test_mapped_tables_are_writable.py pins the 76 with their exact FK counts and ratchets both ends, so no new table can join them unnoticed and the ledger cannot be emptied by deleting mappers.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_mapped_tables_are_writable.py in the unit CI job. The invariant is static and needs no database — the question is whether a mapper's declared targets exist in its own metadata, answerable from the registry alone. Five tests: the probe walked the registry (floor 700 of a measured 716); no undeclared table is unwritable; no ledger entry has been repaired without being removed; the per-table FK counts stay exact; and the writable population never shrinks (floor 630 of a measured 640). Three negative proofs, sources restored byte-identical — including adding a cross-base ForeignKey to trust_sovereignty_rules, which is currently writable, and watching it be caught.
findings.acceptance_criteria: DECLARED_UNWRITABLE is empty and MINIMUM_WRITABLE has risen to the full mapped population.
findings.regression_risk: None from this change — measurement only.
findings.blocker: NR-078's topology change, which is itself blocked on the NR-080 drift reconciliation.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — real Session, real model instance, real flush against PostgreSQL 16 at migration head; plus a static registry walk cross-checked against NR-078's independent count

findings.category: Parallel write authority / Dead code disposition / Latent security defect
findings.status: DISPOSITION ESTABLISHED — RETIRE is safe and ACTIVATE-AS-IS is unsafe; both proved by execution. Retirement itself is the user's call.
findings.title: app/reference is a second, raw-SQL write authority over the three core clinical tables; it is unmounted and schema-incompatible, and activating it as written would store plaintext national IDs
findings.description: app/reference/infrastructure/repositories.py issues raw INSERT and SELECT statements against patients, lab_orders and lab_results — the three most sensitive tables on the platform — through app.database.get_db, i.e. the production database, not a fixture or a separate store. It is a complete parallel persistence stack (domain models, services, repositories, three routers) that duplicates the canonical one. NR-081 asked whether it should be activated or retired. Both halves are now answered by execution rather than by route count, which §21 explicitly forbids relying on. It cannot work: every one of its statements names columns the physical schema does not have. And it must not be made to work as written: it writes a raw national ID into patients.national_id with no hashing and no encryption, which the canonical path does not do.
findings.root_cause: The module was written against a different schema generation from the one the migrations actually built — the same Generation-A/Generation-B split as NR-080 and NR-082, but expressed in raw SQL instead of ORM mappers. Because it was never mounted, nothing ever executed a statement, so the divergence was never observed. Its national-ID handling predates the HMAC scheme in app/routes/register.py and was never brought forward.
evidence: REACHABILITY: no include_router for app.reference anywhere in backend/app. Outside its own package it is referenced only by 4 test files and reports/PHASE_10_BACKEND_ENDPOINT_INVENTORY.md (which marks its 7 endpoints IMPLEMENTED_SOURCE but UNVERIFIED). The two apparent production hits (app/national/services/__init__.py, app/national/api/routes/__init__.py) are a different 'reference' — national reference data — and are false positives. No importlib/__import__ plugin machinery in backend/app could load it dynamically: the only such calls are __import__('datetime') and __import__('uuid'). 8 route decorators are declared across the three routers and 0 are served.

TARGET DATABASE: app/reference/infrastructure/dependencies.py:6 — 'from app.database import get_db', used at lines 23, 31 and 44. This is the production session, so the 'it points at some other database' explanation is ruled out.

EXECUTED against PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003, each in its own rolled-back transaction: repositories.py:56 INSERT INTO patients -> ERROR: column "name" of relation "patients" does not exist; repositories.py:211 INSERT INTO lab_orders -> ERROR: column "test_type" of relation "lab_orders" does not exist; repositories.py:314 INSERT INTO lab_results -> ERROR: column "analyte" of relation "lab_results" does not exist.

FULL MAGNITUDE (information_schema, not first-error): patients 4 of 9 named columns absent (name, date_of_birth, address, updated_at — physical is full_name and birth_date, and there is no address or updated_at column at all); lab_orders 5 of 9 absent (test_type, priority, notes, updated_at, performed_by); lab_results 9 of 13 absent (analyte, min_value, max_value, min_critical, max_critical, is_critical, flagged, notes, performed_by). So only 4 of 9, 4 of 9 and 4 of 13 columns respectively exist. This is a different schema generation, not a typo.

READS FAIL IDENTICALLY: the SELECTs at lines 95, 169, 242, 271, 353, 369 and 402 name the same absent columns (name, test_type, analyte), so the module is dead in both directions. This matters because NR-086 established that raw SQL BYPASSES the NoReferencedTableError barrier that stops ORM writes — so schema incompatibility, not that barrier, is what makes this module inert.
NOT-NULL columns with no default that the statements never supply, so even a column-rename fix would still fail: patients.full_name, lab_results.test_name, lab_results.token.

LATENT SECURITY DEFECT: repositories.py:83 binds 'national_id': patient.national_id straight into patients.national_id. patients has no triggers and national_id has no column default, so there is no database-level protection; encryption is application-level (shared.security.encryption.encrypt_national_id, used by app/citizen_platform/identity.py). The canonical path instead HMAC-SHA256s the value with NID_HMAC_KEY into national_id_hash (app/routes/register.py:337-358), and app/models/patient.py does not map national_id at all. A naive activation that fixed only the column names would therefore write plaintext national IDs, violating CLAUDE.md Security Invariant 8.

CANONICAL OWNERSHIP (unambiguous, single owner each): patients, lab_orders and lab_results are all in Base.metadata and no other registered metadata object, verified against the live target_metadata registry.

MIGRATION OWNERSHIP: all three tables are created by migrations/versions/20250322_0000_create_base_schema.py, the immutable bootstrap snapshot (lab_orders is further altered by 20250323_0004_core_enforcement.py). app/reference owns no migration and has never owned one.

PRIOR DECISION ALREADY IN THE REPOSITORY: backend/tests/test_side_door_hardening.py:81-87 asserts that app/reference/routes/patients.py, orders.py and results.py each contain require_permission("system:admin"). The routers were hardened in place against accidental activation rather than retired, so a decision was taken here before and stopped short of removal.
